title: Q-CTRL Executes 100-Qubit Quantum Fourier Transform Using Convolutional Compilation Strategy - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Q-CTRL ran a Quantum Fourier Transform on up to 100 physical qubits on IBM's Heron R3 processor ibm_boston using a 'Convolutional QFT' compilation that removes routing overhead on linear nearest-neighbor layouts, claimed as the largest functional QFT on hardware to date. Process fidelity was 11.4% at 50 qubits and 1.8% at 80 qubits, with the correct answer still the top outcome at 100 qubits.

insights.claim: Q-CTRL executed a functional Quantum Fourier Transform on up to 100 physical qubits on IBM's Heron R3 superconducting processor ibm_boston, resolving periodic signal frequencies across a 2^100-dimensional Hilbert space, which the article calls the largest experimental QFT on quantum hardware to date.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The QFT underpins phase estimation and Shor-type algorithms; scale records here signal progress for both Q-CTRL's software and IBM's hardware.
insights.quote: marking the largest experimental execution of a functional QFT algorithm on quantum hardware to date

insights.claim: Across 20 randomly sampled target frequencies, Q-CTRL's Convolutional QFT achieved readout-mitigated process fidelity of 11.4% at 50 qubits (10.8x signal peak) and 1.8% at 80 qubits (7.5x signal peak), and up to 100 qubits the correct frequency bitstring remained the highest-probability outcome.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Low absolute fidelities show the 100-qubit result is a signal-above-noise demonstration, not a production-grade computation; track fidelity rather than headline qubit counts.

insights.claim: Two-qubit gate overhead from routing interactions across restricted connectivity is a primary bottleneck for scaling subroutines like the QFT, with linear nearest-neighbor (LNN) topologies incurring substantial routing penalties relative to all-to-all architectures.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Connectivity is a key competitive axis between superconducting (restricted) and all-to-all hardware; compilation that neutralizes it narrows that gap.
insights.locator: A primary bottleneck in scaling subroutines

insights.claim: Q-CTRL's compilation eliminates routing overhead entirely on LNN layouts via identity cancellations, matching the all-to-all baseline of n^2 - n CX gates for a full n-qubit QFT and d(2n - d - 1) CX gates for an approximate QFT keeping the d largest rotations.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Software-only gains that erase hardware connectivity disadvantages boost the value of superconducting platforms like IBM's and of compiler vendors like Q-CTRL.
insights.locator: A primary bottleneck in scaling subroutines

insights.claim: Adding a single ancilla qubit and two extra CX gates turns the approximate QFT into a translation-invariant kernel spanning d + 2 qubits that strides along the register, minimizing two-qubit gates in each qubit's causal light-cone and suppressing noise propagation.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Noise-aware circuit structure, not just gate count, is becoming a lever for extracting usable results from noisy hardware.
insights.locator: To optimize execution on physical hardware

insights.claim: Because qubits in the Convolutional QFT spend long idle windows after participating in the kernel, Q-CTRL protected them with crosstalk-suppressing dynamical decoupling combined with 'as late as possible' (ALAP) gate scheduling.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Q-CTRL's error-suppression IP is embedded in the result, reinforcing its positioning as an infrastructure software layer on third-party hardware.
